name: songhay oriental / soñay de Gao / Koyraboro Senni
confidence_why: Heath 1999, the reference grammar built on fieldwork in Gao and the neighbouring towns, finds no lexical tone and no distinctive stress and reports that Nicolaï could not reconfirm his own minimal pairs when they revisited his recordings together, which outweighs Nicolaï 1982's weakly perceptible final-or-penult accent and Prost 1956's initial stress in disyllables, but Heath's chapter is held only in fragments and the three first-hand accounts differ in both type and placement.

catalog_quote: [Nicolaï 1982:281] Type 2: Système accentuel à liberté limitée. Il s'agit du système qui caractérise le songhay oriental où l'accent peut tomber sur la dernière ou l'avant dernière syllabe du 'mot' et n'est jamais réalisé sur la syllabe initiale des trisyllabes. [fn. 11] Cf. K. Williamson [1967] et R. Nicolaï [1978], toutefois l'interpretation synchronique du système prosodique du songhay oriental en tant que système accentuel ou en tant que système tonal mérite une étude plus détaillée que celles qui ont été entreprises à ce jour. [pp. 307-308] ... les distinctions prosodiques en songhay oriental sont faiblement perceptibles et remarquables non pas par une différence d'intensité mais plutôt par une légère différence de hauteur et/ou de tension. [Prost 1956:37, §69 Accent d'intensité] Dans les mots de deux syllabes, la première est en général à la fois accentuée et allongée, mais parfois seulement accentuée sans allongement. Parfois les deux syllabes sont également accentuées. [Heath 1999 §3.9, Google Books snippet] KS, like KCh and DjCh, has no lexical or grammatical tonal distinctions. ... Nicolaï was kind enough to revisit his original recordings in my presence, and we were unable to confirm the minimal pairs that had been previously reported.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Koyraboro Senni (koyr1242) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Nicolaï 1982 (SAL 13(3)), was already held by the project as the full issue with a text and was read in full for the Eastern Songhay passages. It is about word accent in this language: p. 281 classes 'songhay oriental' (= the Gao group, appendix pp. 313-314) as an accentual system of limited freedom with accent on the final or penultimate syllable and never on the initial syllable of trisyllables, derived historically by rule RR12 (p. 305: final unless a contour sat on the last syllable, then penult); fn. 11 hedges whether the system is accentual or tonal, and p. 308 says the distinctions are only weakly perceptible. This conflicts with the other material held by the project: Prost 1956 p. 37 (initial stress usual in disyllables, sometimes level) and Heath 1999 sec. 3.9 (snippet reconstruction: no lexical/grammatical prosodic contrasts; Nicolaï's minimal pairs not confirmable on re-listening; 2002 review: 'does not have distinctive stress'). Landing page and DOI (10.32473/sal.v13i3.107604, full-issue record) confirmed by automated download and. Heath 1999 remains the unobtained deciding modern source (print-only by automated download).

new_statements.quote: Type 2: Système accentuel à liberté limitée. Il s'agit du système qui caractérise le songhay oriental où l'accent peut tomber sur la dernière ou l'avant dernière syllabe du 'mot' et n'est jamais réalisé sur la syllabe initiale des trisyllabes. [p.281] … Dans ce dialecte [songhay occidental] la confusion entre les schèmes prosodiques est complète; les distinctions qui subsistent en songhay septentrional et en songhay oriental n'existent pas. … les distinctions prosodiques en songhay oriental sont faiblement perceptibles et remarquables non pas par une différence d'intensité mais plutôt par une légère différence de hauteur et/ou de tension. [pp.307-308]
new_statements.translation: Type 2: Accentual system with limited freedom. This is the system that characterises Eastern Songhay [= the Gao dialect group, Koyraboro Senni], where the accent may fall on the last or the next-to-last syllable of the 'word' and is never realised on the initial syllable of trisyllables. ... In this dialect [Western Songhay = Timbuktu] the merger of the prosodic schemes is complete; the distinctions that survive in Northern Songhay and in Eastern Songhay do not exist. ... the prosodic distinctions in Eastern Songhay are weakly perceptible, noticeable not by a difference of intensity but rather by a slight difference of pitch and/or tension.
new_statements.citation: Nicolaï, Robert. 1982. Problèmes de dynamique linguistique: recherches en prosodie songhay. Studies in African Linguistics 13(3): 273-324.
new_statements.locator: p.281 (typology, 'Type 2', with fn. 11) and pp.307-308 (§23); Gao named as the illustrating parler of 'songhay oriental' pp.313-314; derivation, examples and rule RR12 in §19-21 pp.303-306. Same text in Nicolaï 1979 thèse (HAL tel-03112733) pp.281, 323-330.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (Nicolai 1982, SAL 13(3)): the p.281 'Type 2: Systeme accentuel a liberte limitee.. jamais realise sur la syllabe initiale des trisyllabes' passage and fn.11 are verbatim on the saved page scan and in the text (lines 2687-2723 of the); the SS23 'Le songhay occidental' passage ('la confusion entre les schemes prosodiques est complete.. faiblement perceptibles.. legere difference de hauteur et/ou de tension') is verbatim at text-layer lines 4007-4021 (pp.307-308). The same wording is in the compilers scanned of the 1979 these (Nicolai1979_ocr_sec6.5, SS6.5.2.1 and SS6.5.2.6, with the Mary White/Gao footnote). One detail: SAL p.306 prints 'Le passage au songhay…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gao Songhay (KS) has a lexically contrastive word accent confined to a two-syllable window at the right edge: each word is accented either on its final or on its penultimate syllable (never on the initial syllable of a trisyllable), the class being a reflex of the former tonal scheme (proto HH, LL, LH -> final accent; HL and H+falling -> penultimate; monosyllables keep a residual two-way high/low contrast). The contrast is weak and realised mainly by pitch/tension, not loudness.
new_statements.exceptions: Nicolaï's own fn. 11 (p.281): 'toutefois l'interpretation synchronique du système prosodique du songhay oriental en tant que système accentuel ou en tant que système tonal mérite une étude plus détaillée que celles qui ont été entreprises à ce jour' -- i.e. whether the Gao system is accentual or residually tonal is left open. Monosyllables retain a two-way (high vs low) contrast (examples p.304: ʒí, ká, bí vs kà, hì, dò, hòy). Prost 1956:37 gives a different, intensity-based picture: in disyllables the FIRST syllable is 'en général' stressed and lengthened, sometimes only stressed, sometimes both syllables equally stressed; syllables after a CC cluster or after ŋ are very weak; tone 'if it exists' is unimportant.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is Nicolaï's 'mot' / unité élémentaire maximale (lexical word in citation form, examples are isolated nouns and verbs); the statement is typological-diachronic (accent classes derived from proto-Songhay tone schemes) rather than a synchronic stress rule, and the author flags the accentual-vs-tonal analysis as unresolved. The modern reference grammar (Heath 1999) was not accessible and may supersede both Nicolaï and Prost.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted primary sources describe the Songhay of Gao, i.e. koyr1242: Prost 1956 is the grammar of 'la langue soṅay' of Gao (the Zenodo record itself glosses it 'also known as Koyraboro Senni'); Nicolaï's 'songhay oriental' is defined (thèse 1979 p.7 map/designations; SAL 1982 pp.313-314) as the parlers of Gao, Bamba, Gourma-Rharous, Gabero, Kel Alkasseybaten, with the parler de Gao as the illustrating variety (fn. p.323 of the thèse: prosodic schemes 'réalisés dans le parler de Gao' checked with Mary White). Not to be confused with Nicolaï's 'songhay occidental' (Tombouctou/Djenné = Koyra Chiini koyr1240, the fixed-accent system) or 'songhay central' (Hombori = humb1243, tonal). SPA 1979 labels the same Prost material 'Songhai, dialect Gao'.

tone_statements.quote: En outre, les langues songhay présentent des divergences typologiques surprenantes pour une famille dont la profondeur historique n’est manifestement pas très importante : certaines (comme le zarma ou le kaado) ont un système tonal, d’autres pas (c’est le cas du koyraboro senni), certaines (comme le koyra chiini) placent l’objet direct après le verbe, d’autres (comme le koyraboro senni) placent l’objet direct entre le sujet et le verbe.
tone_statements.translation: Moreover, the Songhay languages show typological divergences that are surprising for a family whose historical depth is clearly not very great: some (like Zarma or Kaado) have a tonal system, others do not (this is the case of Koyraboro Senni); some (like Koyra Chiini) place the direct object after the verb, others (like Koyraboro Senni) place it between subject and verb.

tone_statements.summary: No tonal system (KS named among the non-tonal Songhay languages).
